newsitem.title: USA: Boeing airplane market share 64 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Boeing airplane market share 64 pct in 1996.

text.p: Boeing Co's Boeing Commercial Airplane Group said Tuesday it led the industry in 1996 with a 64 percent market share for new commercial airplanes with over 100 seats, driven by demand for its popular 737.
Boeing said it ended 1996 with 717 announced orders worth $53 billion. About two-thirds of the orders were for the 737, the world's best-selling airplane.
The company said it estimates it had net orders in 1996 of 559 airplanes worth $42.8 billion when cancellations and conversions to other airplane models are factored out.
Ron Woodard, president of the Commercial Airplane Group, told a news conference that demand for the next-generation 737, which rolled out of the factory in December, was strong.
He said Boeing has 517 rders for the next-generation 737 series, and 3,604 orders for all 737s.
Woodard estimated the Seattle-based company's biggest rival, European consortium Airbus Industrie, had a 32.3 percent market share in 1996, based on 301 net orders worth about $21.6 billion.
He said McDonnell Douglas Corp, which Boeing plans to acquire, had a 3.3 percent market share.
"Our customers put us on top again in 1996 because of the superior value of our complete family of airplanes," Woodard said. "Our goal is to remain number one."
Woodard reiterated Boeing's goal of reaching a two-thirds market share. The company has historically held a market share of about 60 percent and has had a three-year average of about 61 percent.
He said that while 1996 was the company's best in six or seven years, 1997 will be "as good or better than 1996."
Woodard said he sees an uptick in employment in the coming year although nowhere near as much as 1996's 18,000 new hires.
Woodard predicted the next 20 years will bring 15,900 new airplane orders worth $1.1 trillion. About 75 percent of that will be new orders, with the balance to replace existing aricraft.
Spurring that growth will be the Asia-Pacific market, he said, which will determine the market size for "stretch" aircraft with 500 or more seats.

Woodard said Boeing and Airbus differ radically in their estimates for the "stretch" market. Boeing estimates potential orders at more than 500 aircraft, while Airbus hopes for more than double that figure.
Boeing's largest order in 1996 came from AMR Corp's American Airlines for 103 jetliners valued at $6.6 billion, with options on 527 more jets over the next 20 years.
Other major orders included a $4.3 billion order from Continental Airlines Inc for 78 next-generation 737s, and a $4 billion order from Malaysia Airlines for 25 wide-body jetliners.
